summary: Explores what a host could do when it gets an ICMP source quench message. It proposes that each source host's IP module add some delay between datagrams sent to the same destination. The authors call it a "crazy idea paper" meant to start discussion.

eli5.summary: When a road gets jammed, drivers could wait a moment between cars. This memo suggests computers pause slightly between packets when told the road is crowded.

questions: what can a host do with a source quench
how does source quench congestion control work
subtitle: A crazy idea paper: let a host's IP layer space out datagrams more every time a source quench arrives.

tldr.problem: Gateways send ICMP source quench messages when they are overloaded, but the IP specifications leave unclear what a host should actually do about them, and many TCP implementations never react.
tldr.mechanism: SQuID has the source IP module add a delay D between datagrams to the same destination: D grows by a fixed amount when source quenches arrive and shrinks slowly with time. The memo also proposes that gateways start sending source quenches early.
tldr.outcome: The authors present it as an untested idea for discussion, supported only by a simulation model, and they say all of their algorithms oscillate.

today: RFC 1016 is a discussion memo labelled a "crazy idea paper". The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its status is recorded as unknown.

sections.title: The Source Quench Problem
sections.content:
A gateway may discard datagrams when it lacks buffer space, and may send an ICMP source quench to the source host. A destination host can send one too if datagrams arrive faster than it can process them. The message asks the host to cut back its sending rate to that destination until quenches stop, and then increase it gradually again (see RFC 791 and RFC 792).

The memo points out that neither IP nor ICMP defines a clear event to tell higher-level protocols a source quench arrived, so many TCP implementations are never notified and do not react. Some IP nodes also send only one quench per N discarded datagrams (for example N=20), so the sender that gets it may not be the biggest contributor.

The status note calls the memo a "crazy idea paper" where discussion is essential.
sections.eli5: A crowded junction tells drivers to slow down, but many drivers never hear it. This memo asks what a driver could do about it.

sections.title: The SQuID Algorithm
sections.content:
The source IP module has a queue of datagrams and a parameter D, the introduced delay. After sending a datagram, it waits time D before looking at the queue again. Normally D is zero.

On an increase event, D = maximum(D + K, I), with K = .020 second and I = .075 second. An increase event is receipt of one or more source quenches within an event period E of 2.000 seconds, so a burst of quenches counts once. On a decrease event, D = maximum(D - J, 0) with J = .001 second; this happens when S = 1.000 second has passed since the last decrease and there is a datagram to send. A cache of D values is kept for the last M hosts.

The memo found that incrementing slowly and decrementing quickly spent more time overdriving the network, so it chose a substantial increase and a very slow decrease. It also notes this is the opposite of an early draft by one of the authors. Suggested refinements include per-destination queues, caching per network or subnet, basing I on the slowest network's speed, basing S on round trip time, and scaling D with datagram length.
sections.eli5: Each time the computer hears "slow down", it waits a little longer between packets. Then it very slowly goes back to normal.

sections.title: Implementation Ideas and Gateway Behavior
sections.content:
Since IP normally keeps little state, the memo suggests keeping a list of only those destinations with non-zero D. If a destination is not on the list, its datagrams go out at once. When a source quench arrives for a destination not on the list, it is added with D set to I; if it is listed, K is added.

For gateways it proposes early quenching: start sending source quenches before the queue is flooded, at an SQ Keep (SQK) level, but still forward the datagram. At the SQ Toss (SQT) level the gateway should discard datagrams, except ICMP messages, which are tossed only at MaxQ. Quenching continues until the queue falls below a low water mark (SQLW). In the test model these levels were 70%, 95% and 50% of the queue. The gateway should try to quench as many contributors as possible, but only once per contributor per second or two.
sections.eli5: A gateway would start warning senders while its line is getting long, before it has to throw anything away.

sections.title: Simulation and Observations
sections.content:
The authors built a C model of four nodes: two TCP/IP hosts joined to two gateways, with 10 Mb/s LANs and a 56 kb/s wide-area link in the middle. TCP sent fixed 512 byte datagrams, queues held 15 datagrams, and the loss rate was 1 lost datagram per 300 sent. Sending one 512 byte datagram on the 56 kb/s line takes 73 msec.

Results were mixed. All of the algorithms oscillate, and finding just the right delay is not easy. One lost datagram can hurt throughput heavily: in the memo's example with a 35-datagram window and a 2500 msec round trip, the sender drops from about one datagram per 75 msec to one per 6250 msec, over 83 times slower. Bursts of a full window overflow the bottleneck queue, whereas evenly spaced datagrams are less likely to be lost. A sender that spaces its datagrams seems to get better throughput than one that ignores source quench, and early quenching by gateways seemed to raise effective throughput. The model also lacked slow start and ran only file-transfer-like sessions.
sections.eli5: They tested it on a pretend network. Spacing packets out helped, but the right amount of waiting was hard to find, and one lost packet still hurt a lot.

sections.title: Measuring the Initial Delay
sections.content:
Appendix A explains how to pick the starting delay I. It uses the minimum inter-datagram arrival time (MIAT): how long it takes to send an average datagram across the slowest link. For a 512 byte datagram this is 427 msec on a 9.6 kb/s line, 73-64 msec on a 56-64 kb/s line, and 3 msec on a 1.5 Mb/s line.

A host could guess MIAT passively by comparing arrival timestamps of consecutive datagrams from a source, adjusted for their sizes and ignoring fragmented datagrams. No extra traffic is needed, and satellite delay does not affect it. Alternate routes or datagrams taking different paths can give false values.
sections.eli5: To guess a good pause, you watch how far apart packets arrive. The slowest road on the trip sets the pace.

data.title: SQuID rules
data.code:
on increase event:
    D <-- maximum (D + K, I)
    (K = .020 second, I = .075 second)

on decrease event:
    D <-- maximum (D - J, 0)
    (J = .001 second)

increase event: one or more source quenches within E = 2.000 seconds
decrease event: S = 1.000 second since last decrease, and a datagram to send

viz.caption: GATEWAY QUEUE LEVELS IN THE RFC'S DIAGRAM

items.label: Queue full
items.desc: Datagrams are tossed and quenched, even ICMP messages.

items.label: SQ Toss
items.desc: Datagrams are quenched and tossed, but not ICMP messages.

items.label: SQ Low Water
items.desc: Quenching stops when the queue falls to this level or lower.
